stem: A 59-year-old woman comes to the office due to progressive fatigue and occasional heart palpitations over the last 6 months.  The patient has been under a lot of stress recently due to problems at work.  She has no dietary restrictions, eats meat several times a week, and drinks 2 or 3 cans of beer on the weekends.  The patient is postmenopausal and has not noticed any vaginal bleeding, dark stools, or bleeding with bowel movements.  Her BMI is 23 kg/m2.  Hemoglobin is 8.5 g/dL.  Peripheral blood smear reveals pale, microcytic erythrocytes.  Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of this patient's abnormal laboratory findings?​‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌​​​​‌‌​‌​​​‌​​‌​‌​​​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌​​‌​​‌​​‌​​‌​‌​‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​‌​‌​‌​​‌​‌​​‌​​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​​​​‌‌​​‌​​​​‌​​​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​‌‌​​​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​​‌‌​​​‌​‌‌‌‌​​​‌​​​‌‌​‌​‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​​‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌​​​​​​​‌‌​​​‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​​​​​​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​​‌‌‌​‌​​​​​‌​​‌​​​​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌
explanation:
This patient's peripheral smear findings indicate hypochromic, microcytic anemia, which most often arises in the setting of iron deficiency.  Anemia reduces the oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood, causing fatigue; the heart compensates by increasing heart rate and stroke volume, which can be perceived as palpitations.

Because blood is rich in iron, chronic blood loss is the most common cause of iron deficiency in adults.  Men and postmenopausal women lose very little iron each day, which a typical diet easily replaces; therefore, iron deficiency in these patients most often reflects blood loss, particularly from the gastrointestinal (GI) tract (eg, colorectal cancer, peptic ulcer disease, angiodysplasia).

GI blood loss is often occult because slow, intermittent bleeding (eg, from a right-sided colon cancer) mixes into the stool without noticeably changing its color; melena and hematochezia typically require larger-volume bleeding.  Therefore, the lack of dark or bright red stools in this patient does not rule out GI hemorrhage.  Iron studies (including ferritin) should be obtained to confirm iron deficiency, and upper endoscopy and colonoscopy are typically performed to identify a bleeding source and exclude malignancy.

(Choice A)  Chronic heavy alcohol use typically causes macrocytic anemia due to direct marrow toxicity and folate deficiency.  This patient's modest weekend alcohol intake is unlikely to cause anemia and does not suggest an alcohol use disorder.

(Choice B)  Hematologic malignancies (eg, leukemia, lymphoma, multiple myeloma) typically cause normochromic, normocytic anemia due to replacement of normal marrow by malignant cells and release of inflammatory cytokines that trap iron within macrophages and suppress erythropoiesis (ie, anemia of chronic disease).

(Choice C)  Hemolysis often presents with a normochromic, normocytic anemia, although reticulocytosis can raise the mean corpuscular volume.  Iron from red blood cells destroyed extravascularly is recycled by macrophages, so hemolysis does not typically cause iron deficiency.

(Choice D)  The anemia of chronic liver disease is usually normocytic or slightly macrocytic with target cells on the peripheral blood smear.  When microcytic anemia occurs in these patients, it usually reflects iron deficiency from GI blood loss (eg, varices, portal hypertensive gastropathy).

(Choice F)  Dietary iron deficiency mainly affects groups with high iron requirements (eg, young children, menstruating or pregnant women).  Men and postmenopausal women need to replace only the small amount of iron lost each day, which a typical diet (particularly one with meat, a source of well-absorbed heme iron) easily provides.

Educational objective:Hypochromic, microcytic anemia is most commonly due to iron deficiency.  Men and postmenopausal women lose little iron daily, and dietary intake usually meets their needs; therefore, iron deficiency anemia in these patients is most commonly due to chronic blood loss from the gastrointestinal tract (eg, colorectal cancer), which is often occult.​‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌​​​​‌‌​‌​​​‌​​‌​‌​​​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌​​‌​​‌​​‌​​‌​‌​‌​​‌​‌‌​‌‌​​‌​‌​‌​‌​​‌​‌​​‌​​‌​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​​​​‌‌​​‌​​​​‌​​​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌‌​‌​​‌​‌‌​​​‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​​‌‌​​​‌​‌‌‌‌​​​‌​​​‌‌​‌​‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​​‌‌​‌​‌​‌‌‌‌‌​​​​​‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌​​‌​‌​‌​‌​‌‌​​‌‌‌​‌‌​​​​​​​‌‌​​​‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌​​​‌‌‌​​​​​​​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌​‌​​​‌‌‌​‌​​​​​‌​​‌​​​​​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌
